title: Borrow without copying
subtitle: Make ownership work for your hot path

lessons.title: Views, not copies
lessons.task: Return at most n elements, borrowing the original slice.
lessons.hint: Clamp n with min before slicing.
body: A slice is a view into existing storage. &[T] carries a pointer and length; borrowing a subrange does not allocate or copy its elements. Returning Vec<T> would introduce ownership and potentially an allocation.
Bounds still matter: safe slicing checks that the range is valid. Optimizers can remove some checks when they can prove the bounds, but borrowing alone is not a guarantee of faster machine code.
First return a view; then use split_at_mut to express two non-overlapping mutable regions. This exposes the separation to Rust without raw pointers.

steps.title: Prove the regions are disjoint
steps.task: Add 1 to elements before mid and 10 to the rest; clamp mid to the length.
steps.hint: Use split_at_mut, then iterate each half.
body: Two mutable borrows must not overlap while both are live. split_at_mut checks the boundary and returns disjoint slices. The safe API packages a proof that would otherwise require unsafe code.

lessons.title: Parse without owning
lessons.task: Split on the first =, returning borrowed key and value; return None when absent.
lessons.hint: split_once returns slices with the input lifetime.
body: An explicit lifetime connects an output reference to its input. It does not extend the input’s life or add a runtime counter. The compiler rejects a reference that could outlive its owner.
A parser returning slices can avoid allocating one String per field. The tradeoff is retention: a small borrowed field may require keeping a large input buffer alive.
Use split_once to locate a UTF-8-safe delimiter. A byte index that splits a character is not a valid str boundary.

lessons.title: Own only when necessary
lessons.task: Replace underscores with spaces only when needed. Otherwise return Cow::Borrowed.
lessons.hint: Check contains before constructing an owned replacement.
body: Cow<str> can hold either borrowed text or an owned String. It makes a common fast path explicit: return the existing input if no transformation is needed.
Calling to_mut on a borrowed Cow creates owned storage; calling it on an owned Cow reuses that ownership. The enum and branch have costs too, so this is most useful when unchanged inputs are common.
You will inspect the variant, not just the output text. Correct text alone cannot demonstrate that the borrowed path was preserved.

steps.title: Clone only on mutation
steps.task: Append ! through Cow::to_mut and return the Cow.
steps.hint: to_mut gives mutable access to a String, cloning borrowed text if needed.
body: The output now must own its appended text. Cow delays the ownership decision; it cannot eliminate a copy when you genuinely need to mutate borrowed storage.
